title: Mechanical Engineering Basics
summary: Learn the core ideas of mechanical engineering: forces and Newton's laws, work, energy and power, levers, gears and hydraulics, materials and strength, heat, engines and fluids, and design, manufacturing and maintenance. All calculations were checked in code.
audience: School leavers, technicians, apprentices and anyone interested in machines

body.p: Mechanical engineering designs and makes machines and systems that involve forces, motion, energy and heat: engines, pumps, vehicles, farm machinery, air conditioning, manufacturing equipment and robots. It is one of the broadest engineering fields.

list: First law: an object stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless a net force acts on it.
Second law: force = mass x acceleration (F = ma). Accelerating a 1000 kg car at 2 m/s² needs a net force of 2000 N.
Third law: every action has an equal and opposite reaction; a jet pushes gas backwards and is pushed forwards.

body.p: Friction opposes sliding. It is useful in brakes, tyres and belts, but wastes energy and causes wear in bearings and gears, so engineers lubricate moving parts. Weight is mass times gravitational field strength: a 50 kg person weighs about 50 x 9.81 = 490 N.

body.tip: Always draw a free-body diagram showing every force before calculating.

body.p: Work is done when a force moves something: work = force x distance moved in the direction of the force. Pushing a cart with 500 N for 4 m does 2000 J of work.

list: Kinetic energy is energy of motion: ½mv².
Potential energy from height is mgh: lifting a 100 kg load 2 m stores about 100 x 9.81 x 2 = 1962 J.
Energy is conserved: it changes form but is not created or destroyed.
Power is the rate of doing work: power = work / time. Doing 2000 J in 10 s is 200 W.

body.p: No machine is perfect: some energy is lost, mostly as heat and noise. Efficiency = useful output / input x 100%. A pump that receives 1000 W and delivers 800 W to the water is 80% efficient. Improving efficiency saves fuel and money and reduces emissions.

body.tip: Check units carefully: power in watts, energy in joules, and 1 kWh = 3.6 million joules.

body.p: Machines make work easier by trading force against distance. You never get more work out than you put in.

list: Levers: effort x effort distance = load x load distance (about the pivot). A 25 N effort 2 m from the pivot balances 100 N at 0.5 m.
Pulleys: a system with four supporting rope sections lifts a load with about a quarter of the force, but the rope moves four times as far.
Inclined planes and screws spread lifting over a longer distance.
Wheels and axles, such as steering wheels and spanners, multiply turning force.

body.p: When a 10-tooth gear drives a 40-tooth gear, the gear ratio is 40 / 10 = 4. The output turns four times slower (an input of 1200 rpm gives 300 rpm) but with about four times the torque, ignoring losses. Car gearboxes use different ratios for starting and cruising.

Pressure in a liquid is transmitted equally, so a small force on a small piston gives a large force on a large piston. With pistons of 0.002 m² and 0.05 m², a 200 N push gives 200 x 0.05 / 0.002 = 5000 N. Hydraulic jacks, brakes and excavators use this.

body.tip: Mechanical advantage = load / effort; a higher value means less effort is needed.

body.p: Choosing the right material is a core engineering decision, balancing strength, stiffness, weight, cost, corrosion resistance and ease of manufacture.

list: Steels: strong and cheap; stainless steel resists rust.
Aluminium: light and corrosion-resistant, used in vehicles and aircraft.
Cast iron: good in compression and for engine blocks.
Polymers (plastics): light, cheap, easy to mould.
Composites such as fibreglass and carbon fibre: very strong for their weight.

body.p: Stress = force / area. A 10 kN force on a rod of 100 mm² (0.0001 m²) gives 100 MPa. Strain = change in length / original length. Young's modulus (stiffness) = stress / strain; for steel, about 200 GPa. So 100 MPa causes a strain of 100 / 200 000 = 0.0005, and a 2 m rod stretches by 1 mm.
Fatigue, failure from repeated loading below the normal strength, causes many breakdowns, such as cracked axles and shafts.

body.tip: Designers include a factor of safety, so parts are stronger than the expected loads.

body.p: Thermodynamics studies heat and work. Heating water needs Q = mcΔT, where c for water is about 4200 J/kg°C. Raising 2 kg of water by 50 °C needs 2 x 4200 x 50 = 420 000 J; a 2000 W heater would take 420 000 / 2000 = 210 s, ignoring losses.

list: Heat moves by conduction (through solids), convection (in fluids) and radiation (as infrared).
Heat engines, such as petrol and diesel engines and steam turbines, turn heat into work; they can never be 100% efficient.
Refrigerators and heat pumps move heat from cold to hot using work.
Insulation reduces unwanted heat flow in buildings and pipes.

body.p: Fluid mechanics covers pumps, pipes, fans and aerodynamics. Pressure increases with depth, flow through a pipe is limited by friction, and faster flow through a narrow section means lower pressure (Bernoulli's principle), which helps explain aircraft lift and carburettors.

body.tip: Most cooling problems in machines come from blocked airflow or low coolant; check these first.

steps: Develop detailed designs with calculations and drawings (often in CAD).
Refine, manufacture and support the product.

list: Casting, forging and moulding shape materials.
Machining (turning on a lathe, milling, drilling) removes material precisely.
Welding and fastening join parts.
3D printing (additive manufacturing) builds parts layer by layer and is great for prototypes.

body.p: Preventive maintenance (scheduled lubrication, inspection and part replacement) is cheaper than breakdowns. Condition monitoring, such as checking vibration and temperature, catches problems early. Mechanical engineers work in manufacturing, mining, energy, agriculture, vehicles, building services and design consultancies.
Good design also considers safety, cost, ease of repair with locally available parts, and what happens to the product at the end of its life.

body.tip: Keep maintenance records for every machine; patterns reveal failing parts before they break.
